summary: You produced a correct brute-force implementation that passes all visible tests and most hidden tests, but it fails a hidden case consistent with the stated performance constraints. The main gap was complexity reasoning: you asserted O(n) and “already optimal,” but the submitted solution is O(n^2) and will time out at n=1e5.

dimensions.what_to_improve: Align the implementation with the constraints: replace the nested-loop approach with a hash-map single-pass so it remains correct under large-input time limits (the one hidden failure indicates the current approach is not complete under required constraints).

primary_focus: Master the single-pass hash-map (complement lookup) pattern and practice deriving time complexity from nested loops so you don’t stop at an O(n^2) approach when constraints require O(n).
thinking_and_logic: Your approach was the classic brute-force: for each index i, scan subsequent indices j to find a pair summing to target. That logic is correct for functional correctness, but it performs O(n^2) pair checks in the worst case. Despite passing visible tests, the hidden failure is consistent with hitting a time limit at the upper constraint (n=1e5), where O(n^2) is infeasible.
code_assessment: Compared to the canonical optimal solution, your code uses the brute-force nested-loop pattern and misses the key optimization: a hash map from value → index to find the complement in O(1) average time per element. The optimal technique achieves O(n) time by checking whether (target - nums[i]) has been seen before inserting nums[i]. Your solution also claimed O(n) complexity, but the nested loops are definitively O(n^2), which is exactly the pitfall called out in the answer key.

next_steps.action: Re-implement Two Sum using the single-pass hash map (seen values → index) approach.
next_steps.why: It matches the required performance: O(n) time and passes large hidden cases where O(n^2) times out.
next_steps.how: Iterate i, x over nums: let c = target - x; if c in seen return [seen[c], i]; else seen[x] = i.

next_steps.action: Drill complexity analysis for common loop shapes (single loop, nested loops, triangular loops).
next_steps.why: You misclassified an O(n^2) double loop as O(n), which can cause you to ship non-viable solutions under constraints.
next_steps.how: For each snippet, compute the total number of inner iterations as a sum (e.g., Σ(n-i) = O(n^2)) and sanity-check with n=1e5 feasibility.

next_steps.action: Practice the sorted-array variant using two pointers.
next_steps.why: It’s a common follow-up and reinforces choosing a data-structure/pointer pattern based on input properties.
next_steps.how: If nums are sorted (or you can sort with index tracking), use left/right pointers moving inward based on sum vs target for O(n) scan (or O(n log n) with sorting).

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
Simple enough. I'll iterate through the array and for each element scan the rest for the complement. I'll also guard the empty input case.
Done. All the visible tests pass on the first run.
Nice. Can you analyze the complexity of your solution?
It's O(n) — I only have one main loop over the array, the inner scan is just part of processing each element. Space is O(1).
Are you confident about that time bound for large inputs?
Yes, linear. It only touches each element once from the outer loop's perspective.
Alright. Anything you'd improve given more time?
Not really, I think this is already optimal.
